text: ASD-STE100 is not the right general-purpose standard for persuasive writing.
ASD-STE100 is well-suited to safety-critical procedural and instructional technical writing.
ASD-STE100 Issue 9 was published on 15 January 2025 and is maintained by ASD.
ASD-STE100 descends from AECMA Simplified English, which originated in the 1980s in the aerospace industry.
STE consists of two parts: writing rules and a controlled dictionary.
The claude-writing-skills repository's STE skill encodes STE rules without the approved-word dictionary, making it an incomplete implementation of STE.
STE's one-word-one-meaning rule is its most distinctive anti-ambiguity device and requires the dictionary to function.
STE was motivated by the need to serve multilingual (L2) technician readers and reduce translation cost.
STE's comprehension benefits for L2 readers on procedural text are supported by convergent industrial and research evidence.
There is no persuasion research on STE-100, and the persuasion literature identifies devices STE forbids as load-bearing for attitude change.
STE forbids or degrades rhetorical figures, varied sentence rhythm, synonymy for tone, strategic passive voice, metaphor, and narrative voice—all of which are instruments of persuasion.
Readability formulas were designed to estimate text difficulty, not to guide writing, and using them as writing targets is a documented misuse.
A sentence-length variance threshold of CV > 0.4 used in the repository is an ungrounded heuristic with no basis in comprehension research.
The current enthusiasm for STE in AI and writing-tool communities is driven by its machine-operability and rule-based structure rather than its original aerospace safety rationale.
A context router that selects writing techniques based on purpose, audience, and context is the missing architectural piece in the repository.

Gopen and Swan's reader-expectation theory, grounded in sentence-level information placement (topic position, stress position, old-to-new flow), is a high-leverage technique for expository and scientific prose.
Williams' Style: Lessons in Clarity and Grace provides a clarity-and-grace framework for expository prose that preserves voice while improving readability.
ISO 24495-1:2023 is a principles-based plain-language standard focused on readers being able to find, understand, and use information.
Toulmin's argumentation structure (claim, data, warrant, backing, qualifier, rebuttal) is the appropriate primary framework for decision documents and memos.
Rhetorical figures such as metaphor measurably increase memorability and agreement, as shown in Sopory and Dillard's 2002 meta-analysis.
Narrative transportation is among the strongest persuasion effects in the literature and requires devices STE bans.
Strunk and White's The Elements of Style contains factual grammatical errors and has been actively criticized by linguists.
STE's approved-verb list contains approximately 80 verbs.
STE's sentence-length caps differ between procedural and descriptive text types.
STE controls expression but cannot ensure the correctness of the underlying task analysis or procedure content.
The STE skill in the repository should be relabeled to reflect its actual scope as a procedural/technical controlled-language tool rather than a general clear-writing standard.

STE's general syntactic rules (active voice, one topic per sentence, consistent terminology, imperatives for instructions) are transferable as low-cost clarity improvements across most technical writing even without the full dictionary.
Expert native-speaker readers may experience a fluency and naturalness cost when reading STE-restricted prose.
